title: Analysis of bounds for multilinear functions
contribution: Extends three bounding schemes for products of variables to p variables, adds recursive arithmetic intervals (recursive McCormick), and proves that this compact scheme gives the convex and concave envelopes on zero-anchored boxes while the doubly exponential arithmetic-interval scheme is weaker for p >= 4.
problem_entry: Multilinear terms underlie bilinear, quadratic and multiplicative programs and RLT, but envelope results hold mainly on the unit hypercube, which is awkward under branching (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Recursively replace bilinear products by new variables bounded with McCormick planes and interval bounds (rAI), and compare it analytically with AI, Loga and Expo (pp. 3, 7).
assumptions: Boxes with zero lower bounds scaled to [0,1]^p for the envelope theorems (p. 10); Loga needs positive variables (pp. 3, 8); on [1,2]^3 AI exceeds rAI at one point of Table I (p. 21), so 'positive orthant' means zero-anchored boxes (reader's note).
proof_devices: Counting linear pieces of each scheme: AI for p = 4 has 536,870,912 (Thm 1, Remark 1, pp. 5, 7); rAI has 2^(p-1) pieces but only p-1 lifted variables and 2(p-1) inequalities (Thm 3, Remark 2, pp. 7-8)
Envelope proofs by convex combinations of extreme points of a partition of the cube (Thms 5-6, pp. 10-14)
Induction on p for rAI (Thms 7-8, pp. 14-16)
Multinomial expansion with pairwise cancellation for the exponent transformation (Thm 4, pp. 8-9)
Non-dominance proved by a four-point value table (Thm 12, Table I, p. 21)
experiments: none; Conjecture 2 computationally verified for p = 3,...,9 (p. 22)
positioning: Extends Hamed's three-variable schemes to p variables and re-proves the Crama/Rikun/Sherali envelopes with 'new and more intuitive' proofs (pp. 2-3, 10).
writing: Main result in one sentence (p. 3); theorem-proof sequence; each conjecture stated with the observation behind it (pp. 21-22); one-paragraph conclusion (p. 22).
limits_future: Three conjectures open (pp. 21-22); non-dominance off zero-anchored boxes shown only on [1,2]^3 (p. 21); no test inside a solver.

method_links.note: Analytical form: schemes priced by number of linear pieces and lifted variables; AI usable only via column/row generation, while the compact recursive McCormick scheme reaches the envelope; cost is size, not measured time
Weak, motivation only: bounds must hold on whatever box branching produces, not only the unit cube (premise of step 3, rebuild relaxations on reduced boxes)

transferable: Before ranking relaxations by tightness, count each one's linear pieces and the lifted variables needed to write it compactly (Remark 2(ii), p. 8).
Prove non-dominance between two bounding schemes with a small table of values at a few points of one box (Table I, Thm 12, p. 21).
When the comparisons need known envelope results, re-prove them with a short self-contained argument and say so (pp. 3, 10).

quotes.text: This implies that AI may be practically useful only in the context of a column/row generation scheme.
Consequently, the use of the above-mentioned bounding schemes becomes somewhat problematic in the context of branching in branch-and-bound algorithms.

title: Product disaggregation in global optimization and relaxations of rational programs
contribution: Shows that distributing a product over a sum before applying McCormick (product disaggregation) yields the convex and concave envelopes, characterizes exactly where tighter bounds improve them, builds dominating MILP reformulations of 0-1 rational programs, and shows large node and time savings in BARON.
problem_entry: Carries the MIP lesson that larger, disaggregated formulations can be tighter to the continuous product of a variable and a sum, with rational 0-1 programs as application (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Distribute f over the sum, McCormick each bilinear term; the result is the envelope, whereas substituting w for the sum is not (p. 2; Prop. 4.1, p. 9; counterexample p. 10); recursive multilinear enclosers give an exact MILP (R) for 0-1 rational functions (pp. 8-9).
assumptions: Finite bounds; results on general hypercubes (p. 9); (R) needs valid bounds on every intermediate fractional term (p. 9).
proof_devices: NP-hardness of finite bounds on 1/(b0 + sum bj xj) over binaries by reduction from subset sum (Thm 3.3, p. 6)
Envelope as convex hull of the two faces f = fL and f = fU (proof of Prop. 4.1, p. 10)
Numeric point f(2y1+3y2) at (0.5, 1, 0): envelope 1 vs standard bound 0 (p. 10)
Exact region of strict improvement under bound tightening (Lemmas 4.3-4.6, Thm 4.7, pp. 12-13; Cor. 4.8, p. 14)
Dominance by special case: big-M (RM) equals the bilinear envelope with fL = 0, fU = M (p. 16)
Convex-extension theory from the companion paper (Defs 2.3-2.6, Thms 2.7, 2.9, pp. 4-5)
experiments: Three examples in BARON (CPLEX 7.0, MINOS 5.5, tol 1e-6): HS62 root gap -43%, 1,220 to 667 nodes; reactor reload 1,110 s to 649 s; catalyst mixing unsolved in 100 h to solved in 112 min, root gap -68% (pp. 17-21).
positioning: Continuous analogue of MIP variable disaggregation (pp. 1-2, 10); the standard w-substitution (Quesada & Grossmann 1995) is not the envelope (p. 10); dominates Williams 1974, Li 1994 and Wu 1997 (pp. 3, 16).
writing: Contribution in one introduction sentence (p. 2); a numeric three-variable point proves strict improvement (p. 10); no conclusions section (ends with Example 3, p. 21).
limits_future: Bounding fractional terms is NP-hard, so per-node reformulation may be intractable; polynomial bounding only in special cases (Charnes-Cooper, Megiddo) (pp. 14-15); (R) is not the hull since the hull of fy - 1 = 0 is non-polyhedral (p. 11).

method_links.note: Thm 4.7 and Cor. 4.8 prove where tighter bounds tighten the relaxation; the paper concludes the reformulation must be rebuilt at every node with the tightest derivable bounds (theory under step 3)
Larger LP relaxation accepted with its time effect shown: root gap, nodes, nodes in memory and CPU time per example
Weak: tested inside BARON's NLP module and listed as a BARON lower-bounding scheme (S162 p. 2); primary source for Workflow B2 step 3

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Transfer integer-programming devices into global optimization
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Product disaggregation framed as the continuous analogue of MIP variable disaggregation; Williams-style big-M shown to be the envelope with a weaker bound

transferable: When a relaxation adds variables and constraints, prove the envelope property of the bigger one and give a three-variable numeric point where the compact one is strictly weaker (p. 10).
Characterize the region where a relaxation strictly improves when one bound is tightened (Lemma 4.3, p. 12) to know where bound tightening pays.
Show an older reformulation is your construction with a weaker bound plugged in (big-M = envelope with fL = 0, fU = M, p. 16).
Report each reformulation experiment as root gap, nodes, maximum nodes in memory and CPU time on one machine and tolerance (pp. 17-21).

quotes.text: The main contribution of this paper is to show that this increase in the size of the relaxation comes with an improved tightness as it provides the convex and concave envelopes of (1) over the hypercube.
Therefore, it is critical that the reformulation scheme of Section 3 be applied at every node of the branch and bound tree using the tightest derivable bounds on each fractional term.

title: GAMS/BARON 5.0: Global optimization of mixed-integer nonlinear programs
contribution: The 2002 GAMS/BARON manual documents the branch-and-reduce algorithm (optimality- and feasibility-based range reduction at every node, entirely linear relaxations, branching rules, single-tree K-best search), its history from an 1,800-line GAMS prototype, its model requirements, termination messages and defaults.
problem_entry: Local NLP/MINLP algorithms converge only under convexity; BARON gives global optima under finite bounds on variables and expressions (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Branch-and-bound plus range reduction in pre- and post-processing at every node: marginals and probing, poor man's LPs, factorable relaxations exact at the bounds, sandwich outer approximation, incumbent and periodic bisection branching (pp. 12-26).
assumptions: Factorable functions; finite bounds on all nonlinear variables and expressions, else no global guarantee; no trigonometric functions (pp. 3, 8).
proof_devices: Range reduction from the supporting hyperplane of the convex perturbation function: x_j >= x_j^U - (U - L)/lambda_j (pp. 12-14, Tables 1-2, pp. 15-16)
Poor man's LPs versus 2n exact LPs, with a drawn pathological case (Fig. 5, pp. 16-18)
Worked example on a deliberately weak separable relaxation: 5 iterations; OBRR proves optimality without branching; incumbent branching 3 nodes (pp. 26-33)
Concave QP: bisection branch-and-bound 17 iterations vs branch-and-reduce 7 (pp. 33-36)
Single-cut area guarantee for the projective-error sandwich rule because asymptotic rates say little for few cuts (p. 24)
experiments: No benchmark; two illustrative examples and a screen log (pp. 26-38); declines to predict speed versus other GAMS solvers (p. 46).
positioning: Against local NLP/MINLP solvers via convexity assumptions (p. 1); against other GAMS solvers by two unique capabilities, global bounds and K-best solutions in one call (p. 46).
writing: Tutorial manual: geometric figures for each reduction (Figs 3-5, pp. 14-17), examples traced node by node (pp. 26-36), each termination message explained (p. 39).
limits_future: Missing bounds: may not be globally optimal; numerical difficulties to be reported to developers (p. 39); K-best in continuous spaces only for isolated solutions (p. 26); defaults: LP relaxation, no probing, root LPs and SDPs on (pp. 40-45).

method_links.note: Reduction at every node, ordered by cost: cheap poor man's LPs at nodes, exact 2n LPs once at the root; probing needs extra relaxations and is off by default; passes capped by maxredpass/maxnodepass
1,800 lines of GAMS (1991-93) to a user-configurable experimentation system; still serves for experimentation; algorithms listed by the group's papers; callable library kept
Entirely linear outer approximation justified by NLP unreliability; linear relaxation is the default (nlpdolin 1)

transferable: Run a manual's worked example on a deliberately weak relaxation and switch on one device at a time so each device's effect shows in node counts (pp. 28-33).
Pair an expensive exact reduction run once at the root with a cheap iterated approximation at every node, and draw the case where the cheap one fails (pp. 16-18).
When a guarantee is only asymptotic, prove one for the regime the code actually runs in (a single added cut) (p. 24).
Give every way a run can end its own termination message, saying what it means for globality (p. 39).

quotes.text: Declaration of an inferior solution as optimal by a convex programming solver is fatal in the application of branch-and-bound to global optimization problems.
It still serves as a system that facilitates experimentation with novel branch-and-bound algorithms for global optimization.

title: An approximation scheme for stochastic integer programs arising in capacity expansion
contribution: Gives a three-phase LP-based heuristic (LP relaxation, temporal capacity shifting, capacity bundling) for multi-stage stochastic capacity expansion with fixed charges and proves its optimality gap per period vanishes almost surely as the horizon grows, with computations on 170 instances.
problem_entry: Capacity-expansion models were restricted to linear costs or limited uncertainty; later-stage integers defeat nested Benders and progressive hedging, and no practicable exact method exists (pp. 2-4, 9).
key_idea: Relax integrality (LP, non-anticipative), then relax non-anticipativity and shift capacity to earlier periods per scenario, then restore non-anticipativity by capacity bundling and round (pp. 9-16).
assumptions: Fixed charges, scenario tree from sampled paths, no inventory or disposal; i.i.d. or bounded-support demands and costs; artificial expensive facility for feasibility; unit cost and demand >= 1 for the relative result (pp. 8, 16-18, 23).
proof_devices: Structural lemma: shifting adds at most one expansion per facility beyond the LP (Lemma 3.4, p. 14)
Instance family where naive round-up needs n setups and shifting at most 2 (p. 15)
Extreme order statistics limits (Lemmas 4.1-4.2, p. 19) giving (zH - zIP)/n -> 0 w.p. 1 (Thm 4.6, p. 22)
Feasible LP dual showing zIP = Omega(n) for the relative error (Cor. 4.9, pp. 23-24)
experiments: 170 random instances on four process networks, CPLEX 7.0 defaults as exact baseline: ~1% gap on large instances, exact up to 14x slower; industrial network n = 8 unsolved by IP in 12 h, heuristic 10.7% from LP bound in < 16 min; LP rounding far worse (pp. 24-27).
positioning: Against stochastic-control and two-stage models and multi-stage SLP methods that cannot handle later-stage integers (pp. 3-4); generalizes Rajagopalan et al. 1998 and Chen, Li & Tirupati 2001; earlier heuristics lacked performance analysis (pp. 4-5).
writing: Guarantee in the abstract (p. 2); construction properties 'obvious from the construction' (p. 13); the LP-relative gap caveat written out (p. 26).
limits_future: Guarantee asymptotic in periods only (p. 22); only LP-relative gap for the industrial case (p. 26); cost-aware shifting and hybrid heuristics left undone (p. 16).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Heuristics with proven guarantees, paired with relaxation bounds (science of heuristics)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: LP-based heuristic with an almost-sure asymptotic optimality proof, the LP bound reported on every run; part of a line of such papers (Liu & Sahinidis 1997; Ahmed & Sahinidis 2000a, b). Fits Research Taste mark 3 and Heuristic 7; the Honest Boundary lists this program as claimed but unverified

transferable: Build a feasible solution by relaxing two hard constraint families in turn (integrality, then non-anticipativity) and repairing each in its own phase (pp. 9-16).
Isolate the one structural lemma that bounds the heuristic's excess over the relaxation, then let probabilistic limits do the rest (pp. 14, 19-23).
Show with a parametric instance family that the naive rounding baseline is unboundedly bad, and confirm it on the test set (pp. 15, 27).
When the exact solver fails, report the gap to the LP bound and say that it is that gap (p. 26).

quotes.text: Through probabilistic analysis tools, we prove that the optimality gap of the heuristic solution almost surely vanishes asymptotically as the problem size increases.
It should be noted that the gap of 10.7% is with respect to the LP relaxation value.

title: Design of alternative refrigerants via global optimization
contribution: Formulates refrigerant design as an MINLP with new structural feasibility constraints and finds all its feasible solutions in one branch-and-reduce tree in BARON (45 min, versus 150 h without proof in the mid-1990s), rediscovering CFCs and naming nine compounds not found before.
problem_entry: Molecular design combines combinatorial explosion with nonlinear property models that trap local search; earlier MINLP work was local and interval bounds were weak (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Write structural constraints with integer and 0-1 variables so mathematical-programming bounds exist, add constraints that remove counterexample group sets, and enumerate all feasible solutions in one tree with a problem-specific forward-pass bounding step (pp. 3, 7-11).
assumptions: Joback-Reid group contributions; R12 property targets; generous bounds (15 per group); objective chosen for consistency with earlier work; 52 integer, 14 binary, 21 continuous variables (pp. 4-5, 9-10).
proof_devices: Counterexample group combinations that pass older structural constraints but are chemically infeasible, each removed by a new constraint (pp. 7-9)
Constraint disaggregation for tighter relaxations, 92 to 236 constraints (p. 10)
All-solutions fathoming with optimality-based reduction switched to a linear-relaxation bound (p. 11)
experiments: BARON with two problem-specific modifications, CPLEX 6.0, RS/6000: 150 h for a few solutions without proof (mid-1990s) to 45 min for all, credited to seven developments; 44 solutions, 29 admissible, nine new (pp. 11-13).
positioning: Reviews explicit enumeration (Gani), local MINLP (Macchietto, Achenie), interval bounding with interactive heuristics (Joback & Stephanopoulos) and stochastic search; lists five open issues and resolves the local-optima one (p. 3).
writing: Two numbered contributions (p. 2); formulation remarks that state arbitrary choices (p. 10); candid note that the new compounds seem unfit (p. 13).
limits_future: New compounds likely unstable or toxic; model gives groups not bonding; group-contribution inaccuracy; future: other molecule classes, richer group contributions, larger spaces, relaxed targets (pp. 10, 13).

method_links.note: All/K-best capability added to general-purpose BARON after it worked here; progress told across solver generations (150 h to 45 min). Variant on step 6: same hardware for the mid-1990s runs not stated
Root presolve cuts group bounds from 15 to 5; probing at every node; interval propagation in constraint order collapses continuous bounds as integer ranges shrink
LP-only relaxation eliminated convex NLP relaxations that current NLP codes find hard

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Transfer integer-programming devices into global optimization
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Logical structural conditions modelled with integer and 0-1 variables so mathematical-programming bounds exist; constraint disaggregation for tighter relaxations

transferable: For each set of necessary-condition constraints, exhibit one infeasible object that passes it, then add the constraint that removes it (pp. 7-9).
If fixing the integers makes the continuous variables computable in one forward pass, use rounding plus that pass as the node's incumbent search instead of a local NLP solve (p. 11).
Enumerate all feasible or K best solutions in one branch-and-reduce tree by fathoming only infeasible or point nodes (p. 11).
Credit a speed-up to the list of developments that produced it (p. 12).

quotes.text: The capability to identify all, or the K best, solutions of an integer program was added to the general purpose BARON solver after successful implementation in the context of this molecular design problem.
Interval relaxations are weaker than mathematical programming bounds and, in general, require significant computational effort.

title: An integer programming approach to the phase problem for centrosymmetric structures
contribution: Reformulates the minimal-principle phase problem for centrosymmetric crystals exactly as a linear integer program, solved globally by CPLEX, and determines 18 literature structures with lower objective values and crystallographic R than Shake-and-Bake and CRUNCH.
problem_entry: The minimal principle is a nonconvex trigonometric NLP attacked by local and stochastic search; centrosymmetric phases are 0 or pi but no method exploited it (76% of CSD structures); 1000 MINOS runs miss the global solution (pp. 2, 4).
key_idea: Binary substitutions for the cosines and the normalized phases plus a parity binary give an equivalent ILP with 2T + M variables and T constraints, solved by LP-based branch-and-bound with no starting point (pp. 4-6).
assumptions: Equal atoms in Cochran's distribution; centrosymmetry; atomic-resolution data; N:M:T = 1:10:100 where data allow (pp. 3, 6).
proof_devices: Exact equivalence reformulation of the minimal principle into an ILP (p. 4)
Branch only on the phases and one auxiliary family; the other is integral at the LP optimum because of positive objective coefficients (p. 5)
Finiteness from the finite search space (p. 5)
Multistart histogram to demonstrate the local-optima trap (Fig. 1, p. 4)
experiments: Parametric N:M:T study (Table 1, pp. 4-5); 18 structures all solved, ~2 min average (p. 6); vs Shake-and-Bake (1-1000 trials, expected time) and CRUNCH at defaults: IP time ~30% above SnB expected time, objective 13x smaller than SnB1000, R 55% and 12% better; SnB missed 5, CRUNCH 3 (pp. 6-7).
positioning: Against Shake-and-Bake, CRUNCH, simulated annealing and genetic algorithms, all local or stochastic; credits Shake-and-Bake with showing the minimal principle's usefulness (pp. 2-4).
writing: Abstract states guarantee and scope (p. 2); results organized by three stated purposes (p. 5); conclusions repeat percentages and pose an open question (pp. 7-8).
limits_future: Whether the global minimum is the correct structure for larger and noncentrosymmetric cases is open; specialized combinatorial algorithms and the noncentrosymmetric extension in progress (pp. 7-8).

method_links.note: Certified global optimum is the yardstick showing the incumbent method returns local minima; baselines at defaults with sensitivity checks (10,000 trials, 1.5x invariants); but the own method is the subject from the start, not a neutral benchmark preceding it

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Transfer integer-programming devices into global optimization
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: A discrete property of the application (phases 0 or pi) turns the nonconvex model into an exact ILP solved by a commercial MIP code; also Heuristic 1 (special class first, p. 8)

transferable: Before proposing a global method, show the local-optima trap with many random-start local searches and plot their objective distribution (p. 4).
Look for a physical property that makes a continuous variable discrete and linearize exactly with binaries (p. 4).
Fix data-size ratios by a parametric study before the main runs and use one ratio throughout (pp. 5-6).
For a stochastic baseline, report several trial counts and the expected time to its best, and test whether more trials or inputs would rescue it (p. 7).

quotes.text: While this, effectively, makes the phase problem a discrete optimization problem, no current solution strategy exploits the mathematical properties of the problem to effectively resolve the phase problem.
Obviously, SnB is reporting local minima of the minimal principle model for all of these 18 structures.

title: BARON: The GAMS solver manual
contribution: The GAMS/BARON 6.0 manual chapter (dated 25 Nov 2003) documents model requirements, solver-only bounds and priorities, the log, termination messages and options; read against the 5.0 manual it records changed defaults (probing on every third level, tighter absolute and looser relative tolerance, more root local searches) without stated reasons.
problem_entry: As in 5.0: global optima under finite bounds on variables and expressions (p. 1).
key_idea: User manual, no new algorithm: QCP/MIQCP types, x^y and |x| allowed, option-file solver bounds and priorities, dynamic branching and local-search defaults (pp. 2, 5-9).
assumptions: Finite bounds required, inferred if possible, else no guarantee; additional model constraints may be required; no trigonometric functions (p. 2).
positioning: n/a (user manual); refers users to the 6.0 user's manual and the 2002 book (p. 5).
writing: Option tables with defaults; termination messages with remedies (pp. 4-5).
limits_future: Defaults changed from 5.0 without reasons: pdo -1 with pfreq 3, numloc 10, epsa 1e-9, epsr 0.1, basis saving on, InfBnd 1e4; root SDP option no longer listed (pp. 7-12 vs S162 pp. 40-45); with epsr 0.1 a 'Successful Termination' can mean up to 10% relative gap (reader's inference, pp. 4, 7).

method_links.note: Probing on by default but rationed by tree level (pstart, pend, pfreq 3) and passes capped (maxredpass 10, maxnodepass 5): rationing by a fixed schedule, not an adaptive rule
Dated, versioned document with build stamp, but defaults change between 5.0 and 6.0 with no stated reason or changelog, unlike the later release notes

transferable: Give users a channel for solver-only variable and expression bounds that stays out of the model (p. 6).
Ration an expensive node operation by tree depth (start level, end level, frequency) and expose the schedule as options (p. 10).
When citing a solver result, record the version and the defaults in force; consecutive manuals differ in tolerances and probing (pp. 7, 10).

quotes.text: In order to achieve convergence to global optimality, additional model constraints may be required.
additional constraints have to be provided to BARON, which should be viewed as solver bounds and should not be part of the original model.

title: Approximation algorithms for the minimum number of matches problem in heat exchanger network synthesis
contribution: Introduces performance-guarantee analysis to process synthesis with five approximation algorithms for the strongly NP-hard minimum-number-of-matches problem, a guarantee valid for any heuristic, and an a posteriori ratio from relaxation bounds; on 29 problems the suite averages within 25% of optimal where CPLEX stalls on five.
problem_entry: Process-synthesis heuristics are justified only empirically and exact optimization explodes; the matches subproblem is strongly NP-hard and well understood, so chosen to illustrate the approach (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: LP, dual LP, Lagrangean and primal-dual rounding plus a greedy rule on the transportation formulation, with a priori (PG) and a posteriori (R_APX) guarantees (pp. 6-18).
assumptions: Sequential HENS with fixed minimum approach temperature; feasibility from the minimum-utility step; constant heat-capacity flowrates (p. 4).
proof_devices: Counterexample refuting the N - 1 rule as an upper bound (Thm 1, p. 17)
Basic-solution nonzero count (upper) and max{m, n} (lower) give a guarantee for any heuristic (Thm 2, p. 18)
A posteriori ratio from the best relaxation bound (R_APX, p. 18)
One stream per interval: PG < 2 and PG -> 1 (Thm 3, pp. 18-19)
experiments: 29 literature problems: PG 1.67-15 (mean 6.45) vs R_APX 1-2.93 (mean 1.79); two certified optimal without IP; CPLEX 7.0 defaults stall on five after 7-41 h; no algorithm dominates; best of suite within 25% on average; under 1 s except primal-dual (pp. 19-22).
positioning: Imports approximation-algorithm theory (Ausiello et al., Hochbaum, Vazirani) into process synthesis; builds on the group's probabilistic-analysis papers; formally refutes the N - 1 rule folklore (pp. 3, 7, 16-17).
writing: Defines heuristic, guarantee, approximation algorithm and scheme up front; states the aim is illustration not a complete method; 'main finding' sentence closes the introduction (pp. 3-4).
limits_future: Open: best possible guarantees, approximation schemes independent of problem size, other HENS problems, special-purpose exact algorithms (pp. 22-23).

method_links.note: Portfolio verdict (no single algorithm dominates; run the whole suite) and CPLEX optima as yardstick with unproven cases marked, but the portfolio is of the authors' own algorithms, not existing software

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Heuristics with proven guarantees, paired with relaxation bounds (science of heuristics)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Empirical, probabilistic and worst-case analyses presented as complementary; every run carries a computed bound and optimality is claimed only where the ratio is 1; continues S029's line into synthesis

transferable: Derive a guarantee valid for every feasible solution from two input-computable bounds, to decide before solving whether a heuristic suffices (p. 18).
Report a priori and a posteriori ratios side by side; where the a posteriori ratio is 1, claim optimality without an exact solve (pp. 18, 20).
Test a folklore target with the smallest counterexample before using it as a bound (p. 17).
Introduce a new analysis paradigm to a field on its best-understood hard subproblem (p. 3).

quotes.text: Although the use of heuristics has been prevalent in the process synthesis literature, their justification has been exclusively based on empirical evidence obtained through computational testing.
As seen in Tables 3 and 4, no single approximation algorithm dominates all others for the entire data set.
